paragraphs: Concept unlearning changes a text-to-image diffusion model so that it becomes less able to generate a selected concept. Many existing methods train the denoiser to produce similar outputs when conditioned on the unwanted concept and an anchor concept. This paper shows that their usual squared-error objective implicitly corresponds to a particular divergence between Gaussian distributions.

The authors expand that objective into a framework covering any f-divergence, a family of ways to measure differences between distributions. The familiar squared-error loss becomes one instance. A family of alpha-divergences also gives closed-form Gaussian expressions that remain inexpensive to train with. For other divergences, the framework supplies a variational min-max objective.

The paper analyzes and numerically checks how divergence choice changes gradient strength and convergence, which in turn affects unlearning. Its Hellinger-based instance consistently outperforms squared error in the scenarios examined. The contribution is therefore both a common mathematical description and a practical choice of objectives for balancing removal of a concept against preservation of generation quality.
icml-2026-a-unified-framework-for-diffus.tldr: A unified family of diffusion unlearning objectives offers finer control over concept removal and generation quality.

paragraphs: Multiple-choice tests can reward habits that have little to do with understanding the question. Using a synthetic benchmark called NonsenseQA, this paper finds that language models differ in how strongly they rely on option positions, answer labels, and patterns in the correct answers shown in prompt examples. These influences can also act together.

The proposed evaluation protocol changes how answers are presented and returned. It uses uniform, unordered labels and asks the model to provide the complete answer text. A sentence-similarity model then supports matching the response to the available answers. This reduces the opportunity for arbitrary labels and ordering to drive the result.

Across multiple models and benchmarks, the protocol makes scores more stable when answer options are rearranged. The authors report a threefold reduction in mean accuracy variance, with only a small decrease in average performance. Ablations involving different embedding models and similarity functions support the method's robustness. The resulting scores better expose capabilities under reduced evaluation artifacts.
icml-2026-abcd-all-biases-come-disguised.tldr: Changing multiple-choice labels and requesting full answer text reduces evaluation bias and makes scores more stable across answer orderings.

paragraphs: Claims about the theoretical power of recurrent language models can appear contradictory. Some results give them the capabilities of a general-purpose computer, while others restrict them to recognizing regular languages. This paper attributes the discrepancy to different assumptions about the arithmetic used inside the recurrence. Those assumptions change what the model can represent and compute.

The authors develop a unified account that first specifies the arithmetic model and then translates expressivity into algebraic questions. One such question concerns a relationship between a language's syntactic monoid and a wreath product. This provides a common mathematical framework for comparing results that otherwise seem to describe incompatible capabilities.

A case study makes the importance of arithmetic concrete. A diagonal state-space architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter when its recurrence uses floating-point arithmetic, yet the same architecture can implement every such counter under unsigned-integer quantization. The result shows why expressivity claims need to identify the numerical rules as well as the network architecture.
icml-2026-an-algebraic-view-of-the-expre.tldr: An algebraic framework explains how arithmetic choices can fundamentally change a recurrent model's computational expressivity.

paragraphs: Direct preference optimization trains language models using preferences between responses. This paper revisits the order of assumptions in its mathematical derivation. In the commonly used formulation, a response-level Bradley–Terry preference model comes first, and the reference and trainable language models are treated as autoregressive afterward. The authors argue that this ordering may restrict the framework.

Their alternative introduces autoregressive generation before applying the preference model. The resulting method, Autoregressive DPO, incorporates the sequential nature of text generation directly into the derivation. Its loss has a compact difference from standard DPO: the summation moves outside the log-sigmoid function. The authors derive this change while maintaining the theoretical foundations of the formulation.

The analysis also distinguishes token length from feedback length, identifying two separate length measures relevant to preference optimization. The paper's contribution is a theoretical reformulation and an account of these measures' implications. It gives designers another way to reason about how preference feedback interacts with autoregressive modeling when constructing DPO-based algorithms.
icml-2026-autoregressive-direct-preferen.tldr: ADPO derives preference optimization with autoregressive modeling built in from the start and distinguishes token length from feedback length.

paragraphs: Retrieval systems often use cheap similarity estimates to select candidates before applying more expensive processing. Errors at this early stage affect which candidates remain available later. This paper studies binary cosine sketches, which compress random projections into sign bits. Their usual estimator has especially high variance when vectors are nearly perpendicular, a difficult region for separating candidates from background.

QA-Cos changes the decoder used to interpret those bits. Instead of treating matching signs as deterministic votes through Hamming agreement, it treats the bits as probabilistic observations and uses information from the query. The approach targets the estimation step that drives early candidate selection.

In simulations and BEIR evaluations, QA-Cos reduces estimation error by up to roughly 15–20% near perpendicularity. Reported retrieval gains reach about 30 percentage points in Hit@K at fixed budgets, or roughly 45–50% fewer candidates at fixed recall. A scorer replacement also improves the final HNSW frontier, while a gated variant reduces total latency in a focused storage-aware setting.
icml-2026-beyond-hamming-query-aware-dec.tldr: A query-aware probabilistic decoder improves binary cosine estimates and translates those gains into more efficient candidate retrieval.

paragraphs: Interpreting an image personally requires connecting it to the particular experiences a user has accumulated. This paper formalizes that challenge as contextualized visual personalization. A vision-language model must recognize relevant visual experiences and retrieve their associated textual information when responding to a new image. General visual understanding alone does not provide that connection.

The proposed framework, CoViP, uses personalized image captioning as a central training task. It combines reinforcement-learning-based post-training with caption-augmented generation to improve how models use personal visual and textual context. The authors also introduce diagnostic evaluations that rule out solutions based only on textual shortcuts, allowing them to test whether visual context contributes to the response.

Experiments find substantial limitations in existing open-source and proprietary vision-language models. CoViP improves personalized captioning and produces gains across downstream personalization tasks. These results support captioning as a useful foundation for connecting new visual inputs to a user's previous experiences, with benefits extending beyond the captioning task itself.
icml-2026-contextualized-visual-personal.tldr: CoViP improves visual personalization by training models to connect new images with a user's accumulated visual and textual experiences.

paragraphs: Coreset selection reduces training cost by keeping a small, representative portion of a dataset. This paper adapts that problem to object re-identification, where models must recognize the same person or vehicle across observations. It formulates selection as a joint decision about which classes to retain and which examples to keep from those classes.

The central insight is that diversity within a class matters for a useful re-identification subset. The proposed method first removes classes with little feature diversity, freeing storage for more informative classes. It then greedily selects examples to cover the remaining classes' feature variation, processing classes in an easy-to-hard order.

These two stages are called Diversity-driven Class Pruning and Coverage-Prioritized Sampling. Experiments on three person re-identification datasets and one vehicle dataset show consistent improvements over existing coreset-selection approaches. The findings support allocating a limited data budget according to within-class variation, rather than treating the choice of classes as fixed before selecting individual examples.
icml-2026-csor-coreset-selection-for-obj.tldr: CSOR builds better re-identification training subsets by pruning low-diversity classes and selecting examples that cover variation within the remaining classes.

paragraphs: Atomic facts in sequence models are often understood as associations between entities that appeared together during training. This paper identifies another form of storage: embeddings that encode global relationships across entities, including pairs never observed together. The authors call this geometric memory because relationships are organized through the structure of the embedding space.

That organization can simplify reasoning. The paper demonstrates how a task requiring repeated composition can become a learnable single navigation step when the relevant relationships are represented geometrically. It also finds that this geometry can emerge even when it is more complex than storing local associations, challenging a straightforward explanation based on simpler memorization.

The authors argue that familiar supervisory, architectural, and optimization pressures do not readily account for the phenomenon. Through a connection to Node2Vec, they identify a spectral bias that can generate geometry despite the absence of several such pressures. The analysis also points to room for making Transformer memory more geometric, motivating a reconsideration of how stored facts support knowledge acquisition and reasoning.
icml-2026-deep-sequence-models-tend-to-m.tldr: Sequence models can organize facts into global embedding geometries that simplify reasoning, with a Node2Vec connection revealing a possible underlying spectral bias.

paragraphs: Reasoning across several images requires linking information seen from different viewpoints. This paper draws on two mechanisms suggested by cognitive studies: recognizing regions that refer to the same physical location, and working through viewpoint changes step by step. Existing training approaches, the authors argue, often provide only partial or implicit support for these mechanisms.

HATCH trains both abilities explicitly through complementary objectives. Patch-Level Spatial Alignment encourages representations of corresponding image regions to align across views. Action-then-Answer Reasoning requires the model to produce viewpoint transition actions before giving its final answer. Together, the objectives connect visual correspondence with an explicit sequence of spatial transformations.

Across three benchmarks, HATCH consistently outperforms models of comparable size by a clear margin and is competitive with much larger models. It also preserves single-image reasoning capabilities. The findings support teaching both where views overlap and how viewpoints change, rather than expecting multi-image spatial reasoning to emerge entirely from supervision on final answers.
icml-2026-from-correspondence-to-actions.tldr: HATCH improves multi-image spatial reasoning by explicitly teaching cross-view correspondence and stepwise viewpoint transformations.

paragraphs: A long generated answer contains facts whose relationships matter alongside their individual content. This paper argues that uncertainty measures can miss that structure when they assign one confidence score to a paragraph or compare extracted facts without explicitly modeling their dependencies. Different answers to the same prompt may vary in both what they say and how their claims connect.

GAUSS represents each generated paragraph as a semantic graph. Atomic facts form the content of the graph, and relations capture connections among them. The framework treats structural and semantic discrepancies between graphs from different generations as a source of uncertainty specific to extended outputs.

Its uncertainty measure is the expected cost of aligning an anchor paragraph's graph with graphs from alternative generations. This makes disagreement about relationships part of the score, alongside disagreement about factual content. The proposed framework offers an interpretable account of uncertainty grounded in graph comparisons, making the organization of a narrative an explicit part of what is assessed.
icml-2026-gauss-graph-assisted-uncertain.tldr: GAUSS measures uncertainty in long answers by comparing both facts and their relationships across semantic graphs of alternative generations.

paragraphs: Mean field variational inference is commonly described as underestimating uncertainty. This paper shows that the description depends on which uncertainty is measured. In conjugate Bayesian linear regression, the approximation underestimates variance in model parameters, yet it can overestimate the variance of predictions relative to the exact posterior.

The analysis establishes a directional relationship: if predictive variance is underestimated in some directions, it must be overestimated in others. Overestimation occurs in directions where training data concentrates. Consequently, for a test point drawn from the training distribution, the approximation's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior in the analyzed setting.

The authors also demonstrate a pathological case in which predictive variance on independent, identically distributed data does not decrease from its prior level. They connect the findings to the Cold Posterior Effect, arguing that temperature adjustment can correct overestimation and bring predictions closer to exact Bayesian results. Synthetic and real-world regression experiments validate the theory, refining how uncertainty from this approximation should be interpreted.
icml-2026-gaussian-mean-field-variationa.tldr: In Bayesian linear regression, mean field inference can underestimate parameter variance while overestimating predictive variance where training data concentrates.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether mathematical reasoning can be assessed through a transformer's internal attention patterns. It treats each attention matrix as a weighted graph connecting tokens and extracts four spectral diagnostics: Fiedler value, high-frequency energy ratio, spectral entropy, and smoothness. These measurements require no learned parameters, offering a training-free signal for distinguishing valid reasoning.

Across seven models from four architectural families, single-threshold classification reaches 85–96% accuracy. The signal follows logical coherence closely enough to recognize valid proofs rejected because of timeouts or missing imports, with support from a manual audit. Attention architecture also matters: sliding-window attention shifts the useful diagnostic from high-frequency energy toward smoothness.

Causal ablations trace the signature to induction-head circuits. The authors also report generalization to informal chains of thought and improved proof search when candidates are reranked using high-frequency energy. Best-of-16 Pass@1 improves by 4.4–6.6%. Together, the findings support an architecture-aware verification approach whose useful internal measurement depends on the attention design.
icml-2026-geometry-of-reason-spectral-si.tldr: Training-free spectral measurements of attention distinguish valid mathematical reasoning and improve proof selection, with the most useful measurement depending on architecture.

paragraphs: Grokking is the sudden emergence of generalization after a long period of memorization during training. This paper studies it in learning multiplication within finite-dimensional algebras, extending work centered on group operations. The framework includes algebras that need not be associative, commutative, or equipped with an identity element.

The authors show that learning group operations fits within this broader setting. Learning algebra multiplication becomes learning a bilinear product described by a structure tensor. Over the real numbers, they connect the problem to matrix factorization with an implicit preference for low rank. Over finite fields, they show how grokking arises as models learn discrete representations of algebraic elements.

The experiments investigate how algebraic rules influence whether and when grokking appears, how tensor sparsity and rank affect generalization, and whether learned embeddings align with algebraic representations. This supplies a common language for examining delayed generalization across different mathematical structures. It also connects the training phenomenon to properties of the operation being learned and its internal representation.
icml-2026-grokking-finite-dimensional-al.tldr: A finite-dimensional algebra framework connects grokking to multiplication structure, matrix factorization, and learned representations beyond group operations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how AI can refine a human expert's set of plausible predictions while preserving useful human judgment. Two principles govern the collaboration: counterfactual harm concerns degrading correct human judgments, while complementarity concerns recovering correct outcomes the human omitted. The aim is to improve the joint prediction set under both requirements.

At the population level, the authors characterize the optimal collaborative set using two thresholds applied to one score function. One threshold governs pruning the human proposal, and the other governs adding outcomes. This gives a simple structural description of how a system can make a human-provided set more selective while also correcting omissions.

The paper develops offline and online calibration algorithms with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. The online method adapts to arbitrary distribution shifts, including changes in human behavior during interaction. Across image classification, regression, and text-based medical decisions, collaborative sets improve the tradeoff between covering correct outcomes and keeping predictions efficient compared with human-only and AI-only baselines.
icml-2026-human-ai-collaborative-uncerta.tldr: Calibrated AI refinement of human prediction sets improves coverage–efficiency tradeoffs while accounting for harm and complementary corrections.

paragraphs: Noisy-input classification often uses a pipeline that first cleans the signal and then classifies it. This paper argues that separating the stages leaves useful information unused: the classifier's developing interpretation could help decide how to reconstruct the signal. The proposed framework allows enhancement and classification to guide one another during processing.

It couples two diffusion models, one operating on the input signal and another on the classifier's logits, the scores underlying its output. As the signal improves, it refines the class estimate. In return, the evolving class scores guide reconstruction toward regions relevant for distinguishing classes. The framework does not require retraining or fine-tuning the classifier.

The authors introduce three strategies for modeling the joint distribution of signal and logits. Evaluations cover image classification and automatic speech recognition under varied noise conditions, where the coupled approach improves classification accuracy over sequential enhancement baselines. These results support using semantic feedback during denoising within a framework intended to work across domains.
icml-2026-joint-enhancement-and-classifi.tldr: Coupled diffusion models let signal enhancement and class estimates guide each other, improving noisy-input recognition without retraining the classifier.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization chooses decisions that account for uncertainty about the data distribution. In optimal-transport approaches, an ambiguity set describes plausible distributions around the observed data. The usual workflow designs that set first and then optimizes the decision. This paper argues that separating those steps can make decisions excessively conservative.

The proposed method learns the ambiguity set and the decision process together. The downstream loss informs the set's shape, making the uncertainty description sensitive to what matters for the decision. Data-driven bootstrapping enforces distributional robustness while the learned set supports less conservative choices. This links uncertainty quantification directly to the objective it is intended to protect.

The authors formulate the procedure as a bilevel optimization problem and solve it with hypergradients. Using a nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, they establish convergence to a critical point of that problem. Experiments on portfolio optimization and linear regression validate the approach. The theoretical result concerns critical-point convergence, while the practical contribution is learning uncertainty sets around decision-relevant losses.
icml-2026-loss-aware-distributionally-ro.tldr: Learning optimal-transport ambiguity sets jointly with downstream decisions reduces conservatism while enforcing robustness through bootstrapping.

paragraphs: A system of cooperating language-model agents can become unsafe when some agents fail or are compromised. This paper studies how to automate the design of systems that remain safe under that threat. It frames the task as a game between a designer, called the Meta-Agent, and an adversary that selects agents to compromise.

The formulation draws on Stackelberg security games, with the adversary responding to the proposed system design. The resulting MaMa algorithm uses language-model-based adversarial search. The designer repeatedly proposes systems and receives feedback from the strongest attacks the Meta-Adversary discovers, making discovered failure modes part of the design process.

Across the evaluated environments, MaMa-designed systems consistently defend against worst-case attacks while retaining performance comparable to systems optimized only for task success. They also generalize to stronger adversaries and adversaries with different objectives or underlying language models. These empirical results support iterative adversarial design as a way to improve safety beyond the particular attacks used during training.
icml-2026-mama-a-game-theoretic-approach.tldr: MaMa designs multi-agent systems through iterative competition with an adversary, improving empirical resistance to compromised agents while preserving task performance.

paragraphs: Mesh-based physical simulation combines how elements connect with geometric and material information. Mesh Field Theory separates these roles so a learned simulator can preserve physical structure. The paper starts from locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and an energy balance or dissipation requirement, then asks what form the dynamics must take under those conditions.

Its reduction theorem gives a local port–Hamiltonian factorization. The mesh topology uniquely fixes the conservative interconnection, while metric effects enter through constitutive relations and dissipation. This distinction tells the neural realization, MeshFT-Net, which structure to keep fixed and which parts to learn, reducing nonphysical freedom in the model.

Evaluations include analytic and realistic datasets, physical consistency checks, and tests outside the training distribution. MeshFT-Net exhibits near-zero energy drift, correct dispersion and momentum conservation, robust extrapolation, and high data efficiency. The findings support using the theorem's conditional structural decomposition as an inductive bias for learning stable physical dynamics while concentrating learning on metric-dependent behavior.
icml-2026-mesh-field-theory-porthamilton.tldr: MeshFT separates topology-fixed physical structure from learnable metric effects, enabling simulations with strong physical fidelity and near-zero energy drift.

paragraphs: Repeated conversations with AI can change human decisions over several rounds. This paper proposes evaluating that interaction through two human-centered requirements: avoiding damage to a person's strengths and adding value where the person tends to make mistakes. Users specify task-dependent rules defining these notions of counterfactual harm and complementarity.

The authors introduce an online algorithm that enforces the resulting constraints over the collaboration process. It provides distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees, allowing the requirements to guide ongoing interaction without needing a model of human behavior. The framework turns broad goals for helpful collaboration into explicit constraints whose violation rates can be controlled.

Evaluation uses language-model-simulated collaboration on medical diagnosis and a human crowdsourcing study on pictorial reasoning. The procedure maintains prescribed violation rates even when interaction dynamics change over time. Tightening or relaxing the constraints produces predictable changes in downstream human accuracy. These findings make the requirements practical controls for steering collaboration, with the chosen constraints determining how the system balances preserving strengths and correcting errors.
icml-2026-multi-round-humanai-collaborat.tldr: An online framework lets users control harm and complementarity requirements during multi-round human–AI collaboration with finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Semantic caching can reduce language-model cost and latency by recognizing when a new prompt matches a previously cached one. Its usefulness depends on finding reusable matches without accepting incorrect ones. This paper argues that simple prompt-similarity measures miss opportunities for accurate retrieval and proposes a more detailed comparison through MVR-cache.

The system learns how to divide prompts into segments and represents them with multiple vectors. It then uses MaxSim for fine-grained comparisons between prompts. A theoretical analysis supplies the segmentation model's training objective, connecting its optimization to maximizing cache hits under strict correctness constraints. Because the resulting combinatorial problem is not differentiable, the authors train with reinforcement learning using that objective as the reward.

Across established benchmarks covering diverse tasks, MVR-cache consistently improves hit rates over the state of the art, with gains of up to 37% while maintaining the same correctness guarantees. The findings support learning prompt segmentation specifically for reuse decisions, so finer comparisons translate into more usable cached responses.
icml-2026-mvr-cache-optimizing-semantic-.tldr: MVR-cache learns prompt segmentation for multi-vector matching, increasing cache hits by up to 37% while maintaining correctness guarantees.

paragraphs: Skipping selected layers for each token reduces language-model computation, while quantizing weights reduces memory use. Combining these methods directly can cause extra accuracy loss. This paper attributes the difficulty to reduced redundancy: token-adaptive training explores fewer execution paths, and inference activates fewer parameters that might otherwise help absorb quantization effects.

QTALE addresses both sources of reduced redundancy. During fine-tuning, it actively explores diverse execution paths. After training, it allows the execution ratio to change at inference, making it possible to restore redundancy when needed. The method therefore treats the amount of active computation as something that can be adjusted alongside reduced weight precision.

Experiments show that QTALE combines these efficiency techniques with no noticeable accuracy difference in the reported comparison, keeping the gap from quantization-only models below 0.5% on CommonsenseQA benchmarks. The result supports jointly managing training-path diversity and inference execution to obtain computation and memory savings while limiting the additional accuracy cost of combining them.
icml-2026-qtale-quantization-robust-toke.tldr: QTALE combines adaptive layer skipping with quantization by preserving execution-path diversity and allowing inference-time adjustments to active computation.

paragraphs: Data transformations can preserve distances approximately while still changing the decisions produced by a geometric algorithm. For clustering, retaining a similar objective value does not by itself ensure that points receive consistent assignments. This paper focuses on that distinction when constructing compact summaries of data that may later be transformed.

The authors introduce gamma-resilient coresets, building on an existing notion of resilient algorithms. These are weighted summaries designed to provide both a multiplicative approximation to the objective and stability at the assignment level. A gamma-resilient (k, epsilon)-coreset guarantees a factor of 1 plus epsilon for the objective while incorporating the stronger consistency requirement.

The paper pairs its positive result with a lower bound: obtaining a tight approximation for resilient clustering requires a bicriteria solution. Thus, preserving assignments introduces an additional demand beyond preserving numerical cost alone. The contribution makes stability part of the summary's formal specification, addressing a gap between geometry-preserving transformations and consistent downstream clustering outcomes.
icml-2026-resilient-coresets-and-cluster.tldr: Resilient coresets aim to preserve both clustering objective values and assignment stability, with a lower bound requiring bicriteria solutions for tight approximation.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential learning from pairwise comparisons when several complications occur together. Relevant context becomes available only after serving a choice, feedback arrives after unknown delays, and an adversary can corrupt observations within a cumulative budget. The learner must make decisions while accounting for all three sources of difficulty.

RCDP-UCB learns an approximation that predicts post-serving context from information available beforehand. It also adaptively weights observations and clips feature vectors to reduce the combined impact of corruption and delay. The algorithm does not need to know whether delays follow a stochastic or adversarial regime.

Under standard regularity conditions and a parametric post-serving mapping, the authors prove a regret bound scaling, up to logarithmic factors, with feature dimension times the sum of the square root of the horizon, corruption budget, and delay complexity. Delay complexity depends on the delay regime. Lower bounds nearly match the upper bounds within a square-root-of-dimension factor for adversarial delays when post-serving contexts are absent, clarifying the guarantee's scope.
icml-2026-robust-linear-dueling-bandits-.tldr: RCDP-UCB combines context prediction and adaptive observation weighting to provide conditional regret guarantees under unknown delays and adversarial corruption.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks aim to respond consistently when their inputs undergo transformations. Many existing methods handle transformation groups that are finite, compact, or low-dimensional with linear actions. This paper explores diffeomorphisms, a much richer family of smooth, invertible deformations belonging to an infinite-dimensional group.

The proposed strategy adds energy-based canonicalization to pretrained networks. It formulates the equivariance problem as an optimization task, allowing established differentiable image-registration methods to be used. Canonicalization provides a way to handle transformations through this optimization process, extending the available machinery beyond the groups commonly addressed by convolution or averaging methods.

Experiments on segmentation and classification show approximate equivariance and generalization to transformations not seen previously. These results are achieved without relying on extensive data augmentation or retraining. The empirical finding is approximate consistency under deformation, supporting canonicalization as a practical route toward applying pretrained networks to a broader range of transformations while reusing existing image-registration tools.
icml-2026-towards-diffeomorphism-equivar.tldr: Energy-based canonicalization gives pretrained networks approximate equivariance to smooth deformations and generalization to unseen transformations.

paragraphs: Smooth behavior is often studied as a desirable property of transformers, but its role in adapting a pretrained model is less clear. This paper examines vision-transformer components through plasticity: how readily their outputs change when their inputs change. It defines plasticity as an average rate of change, so greater plasticity corresponds to lower smoothness.

The authors combine theoretical analysis with more than 1,000 fine-tuning runs on large-scale vision transformers. They use the plasticity perspective to guide which components should receive priority during adaptation. This connects a component's functional response to input perturbations with its usefulness when the model is transferred to a new task.

A central finding is that the high plasticity of attention modules and feedforward layers consistently leads to better fine-tuning performance. The result challenges a blanket preference for smoothness in this transfer-learning setting. It offers practitioners a principled criterion for choosing adaptation targets based on their capacity to change outputs, supported by both analysis and extensive experiments.
icml-2026-vision-transformer-finetuning-.tldr: Vision-transformer fine-tuning benefits from prioritizing highly plastic attention and feedforward components, whose outputs respond more strongly to input changes.
